q-115261.problem: Given that the tangent line approximation to the function $f(x)$ at $x=\sqrt{2}$ overestimates the values of the function in the neighborhood of $x=\sqrt{2},$ which of the following must be true?
q-115261.worked_solution:
Since the tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at $x=\sqrt{2}$ overestimates the values of the function, we have

$$
L(x)>f(x),
$$

that is, the line $L(x)$ must be above the graph of $f(x)$ near the point  $x=\sqrt{2}.$

Therefore, the function must be concave down in the neighborhood of $x=\sqrt{2}.$

q-123316.problem:
Which of the following sequences diverge?

I. ${a}_{n}=\frac{{n}^{3}}{1-{n}^{2}}$ for $n\ge 1$
II. ${a}_{n}=\frac{3}{n}$ for $n\ge 1$
III. ${a}_{n}=\frac{2{n}^{2}-3{n}^{3}}{{n}^{3}+5}$ for $n\ge 1$
q-123316.worked_solution:
Let's analyze each sequence in turn. We need to calculate the limit of each sequence as $n$ approaches infinity.

- In sequence I,  the dominant term in the denominator is $-{n}^{2},$ so we divide the numerator and the denominator by ${n}^{2}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{n\to \infty }{a}_{n} & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{{n}^{3}}{1-{n}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{{n}^{3}}{{n}^{2}})}{(\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}-\frac{{n}^{2}}{{n}^{2}})} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{n}{(\frac{1}{{n}^{2}}-1)} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{n}{0-1} \\  & =-\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

The limit does not exist, so the sequence diverges.

- In sequence II, the limit is

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }{a}_{n}={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{3}{n}=0.
$$

The limit exists, so the sequence converges.

- In sequence III, the dominant term in the denominator is ${n}^{3},$ so we divide the numerator and the denominator by ${n}^{3}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{n\to \infty }{a}_{n} & =\frac{2{n}^{2}-3{n}^{3}}{{n}^{3}+5} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{2{n}^{2}}{{n}^{3}}-\frac{3{n}^{3}}{{n}^{3}})}{(\frac{{n}^{3}}{{n}^{3}}+\frac{5}{{n}^{3}})} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{2}{n}-3)}{(1+\frac{5}{{n}^{3}})} \\  & =\frac{0-3}{1+0} \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

The limit exists, so the sequence converges.

In conclusion, sequence I diverges.

q-123439.knowledge_point: Constructing Line Integrals of Unity Over Polar Curves
q-123439.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r={sec}^{3}⁡\theta \,$ for $-\pi /2\le \theta \le \pi /2$ ?
q-123439.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r={sec}^{3}⁡\theta \,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=3{sec}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{({sec}^{3}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(3{sec}^{3}⁡\theta \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{-\pi /2}\sqrt{{sec}^{6}⁡\theta +9{sec}^{6}⁡\theta {tan}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{sec}^{6}⁡\theta (1+9{tan}^{2}⁡\theta })\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{sec}^{3}⁡\theta \sqrt{1+9{tan}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

q-123458.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }\,$ for $0\le \theta \le 2\pi $ ?
q-123458.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }\,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡4\theta }{\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡4\theta }}.
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is 

$$

$$

q-126539.knowledge_point: Expressing a Line Integral Along a Circular Path as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem
q-126539.problem:
Given that 

$$
{∮}_{C}x{y}^{2}\,dx+2{x}^{2}y\,dy={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{6}\boxed{}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $C$ is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=36$ oriented counterclockwise, what is the missing part of the equation?
q-126539.worked_solution:
Green's theorem states that 

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/c2/c2718471780b5ea4f4b0298624d14a22efb317ef4e8302b9269eeeec9449ca0d.png)

Since $P(x,y)=x{y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=2{x}^{2}y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=4xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}x{y}^{2}\,dx+2{x}^{2}y\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(4xy-2xy)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2xy\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 6,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2xy\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}2\cdot r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}2{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{6}{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

q-126564.knowledge_point: Expressing a Line Integral Along a Circular Path as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem
q-126564.problem:
Given that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{2}\boxed{}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $F(x,y)=⟨xy-\sqrt[3]{x+5},\,x+2y⟩$ and $C$ is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4$ oriented counterclockwise, what is the missing part of the equation?
q-126564.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}(xy-\sqrt[3]{x+5})\,dx+(x+2y)\,dy.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](images/79/798665574b8f0e11d991bb0d934efd01bdeb65840c2e86498be4edbc59578439.png)

Since $P(x,y)=xy-\sqrt[3]{x+5}$ and $Q(x,y)=x+2y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(xy-\sqrt[3]{x+5})\,dx+(x+2y)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1-x)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(1-x)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(1-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{2}r-{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

q-126748.knowledge_point: Expressing the Area Bounded by a Closed Curve Using Green’s Theorem
q-126748.problem:
![](images/65/6571fcdf94818485c2a39e90e018d46e9c95e1acbe0a8cf2f67c688d160a347c.png)

Let $D$ be the region enclosed by the curve $C$ parametrized as
$r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩$ for $t\in [-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}].$ 
The area of $D$ can be written as

$$
\text{Area}(D)={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})dA={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\boxed{}\,dt,
$$

where $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0.$ Determine the missing part of the equation.

*Hint: Note that $C$ is negatively oriented.*
q-126748.worked_solution:
Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is negatively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0-(-1)=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & =-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Notice that we have to take the line integral with a minus sign since the path is negatively oriented.

Substituting $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0,$ we get

$$
-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}y\,\text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
{r}^{′}(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 4\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

q-161862.knowledge_point: Expressing Flux as a Double Integral Given a Diagram
q-161862.problem:
![](images/e6/e61f3d7c23ef7876bec2f11c93974551058bcd32f28745898604926d84dbcfee.png)

Consider the vector field $F=⟨y,\,0,\,2x⟩$ and the closed surface $S$ that represents the boundary of the solid shown above. Let $D$ be the projection of the solid onto the $xy$-plane. The flux of $F$ across $S$ can be expressed in terms of a double integral as 

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∬}_{D}\,\,\text{d}A.
$$

Which of the following could be the missing expression?
q-161862.worked_solution:
Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So,

- the upper surface ${S}_{1}:z=g(x,y)=0$ is oriented upward, and

- the lower surface ${S}_{2}:z=h(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-2$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

- Consider the upper plane ${S}_{1}.$ 

Since the positive orientation is upward, the unit normal vector to the plane is $n=⟨0,0,1⟩.$ As a result, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨y,0,2x⟩\cdot ⟨0,0,1⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2x\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

- Consider the lower cone ${S}_{2}.$

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=h(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-2)=\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}} \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-2)=\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=y,\,Q=0,\,R=2x.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is downward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & =-{∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂h}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂h}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}(-y\cdot \frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}-0\cdot \frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}+2x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{xy}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}-2x)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux across the entire surface is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}2x\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}(\frac{xy}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}-2x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{xy}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

and equating the coefficients of $i,j,$ and $k$ yields the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t=-1 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t=0 \\ t=\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $t=\frac{3}{2}.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(-1,0,\frac{3}{2})$ is at the tip of the vector $r(\frac{3}{2}).$  

We calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,k \\  & =\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t\,i-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t\,j+\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=\frac{3}{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\frac{3}{2}) & =\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})\,i-\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})\,j+\,k \\  & =0\,i+\pi \,j+\,k \\  & =\pi \,j+\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point $P(-1,0,\frac{3}{2})$ is

$$
R(u)=-i+\frac{3}{2}\,k+u\,(\pi \,j+\,k),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

q-36754.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of the Normal Line to a Surface Using the Gradient
q-36754.problem: Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface ${x}^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{4}=1$ at the point $(0,0,2).$
q-36754.worked_solution:
First, note that we can write the equation of our surface as

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{4}-1=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we set $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{4}-1$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(0,0,2)$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,0,2).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,0,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{4}-1)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{4}-1)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{4}-1)k \\  & =2x\text{ }i+\frac{2y}{9}\text{ }j+\frac{z}{2}\text{ }k \\ ∇f(0,0,2) & =2(0)\text{ }i+\frac{2(0)}{9}\text{ }j+\frac{(2)}{2}\text{ }k \\  & =k \\  & =⟨0,0,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, the vector form of the equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(0,0,2)$ and passes through the point $(0,0,2)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨0,\,0,\,2⟩+t\,∇f(0,0,2)=⟨0,\,0,\,2⟩+t\,⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

q-51252.knowledge_point: Translating Contextual Problems Into Differential Equations
q-51252.problem: A tank is being filled with water. The rate of change of the volume of water in the tank $V,$ in milliliters, is directly proportional to the time $t,$ measured in hours. Additionally, the tank is also leaking $200\,\text{ml}$ of water every hour. What is the differential equation that describes the rate of change of the volume of water in the tank, at time $t,$ where $t$ is the time (in hours) since the tank started filling?
q-51252.worked_solution:
The rate of change in the volume of water in the tank per hour increases in proportion to $t$ and decreases by $200.$ The differential equation that describes this is

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=kt-200,
$$

where $k$ is the (positive) constant of proportionality.

q-72575.knowledge_point: Identifying Augmented Matrices in Row Echelon Form
q-72575.problem:
Which of the following augmented matrices are **not** in row echelon form?

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 4 & 9 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 5 & 5\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 & 0 & -1 & 6 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 & 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$
q-72575.worked_solution:
Remember that an augmented matrix is in row echelon form if its coefficient matrix satisfies the following conditions:

- All the zero rows (rows with only zeros), if any, are placed at the *bottom* of the matrix.
- Each leading entry of a row is in a column *to the right* of the leading entry of the row above it.

With that in mind, let's look at each matrix in turn.

- The matrix $A$ is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

- The matrix $B$ is not in row echelon form since ${b}_{22}\ne 0$ (condition II is violated).

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 4 & 9 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 5 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

- The matrix $C$ is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 & 0 & -1 & 6 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 & 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, only $B$ is **not** in row echelon form.

q-79044.knowledge_point: Identifying When a Circle Does Not Intersect an Axis
q-79044.worked_solution:
We must have $y=0$ at the $x$-intercepts.  

So, we need to substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the circle and solve the resulting equation for $x,$ if possible:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2x+6y+12 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+{0}^{2}-2x+6\cdot 0+12 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-2x+12 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this equation by completing the square, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-2x+1+12 & =0+1 \\ (x-1)^{2}+12 & =1 \\ (x-1)^{2} & =-11\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(x-1)^{2}\ge 0$ for all values of $x,$ there is no $x$ such that $(x-1)^{2}=-11.$ Therefore, circle has no $x$-intercepts, as shown below.

q-79315.knowledge_point: Translating Problems With Proportional Rates of Change Into Differential Equations
q-79315.problem: The rate of growth of a car's displacement increases at a rate that's proportional to the time $t$ since the car started moving. What differential equation describes the rate of change of the car's displacement, $D,$ at time $t?$
q-79315.worked_solution:
Let's highlight the important words in the given statement:

*The rate of growth of a **car's displacement** $D(t)$ **increases** at a **rate** that's **proportional** to the **time** $t$ since the car started moving.*

We note the following:

- The question describes the *rate* at which the *car's displacement* varies. Therefore, this is a statement about the quantity 

$$
\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}.
$$

- We're told that $\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}$ is *proportional to* the *interval of time* since the car started moving. In other words,

$$
\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}∝t.
$$

Recall that $∝$ means "is proportional to."

- Finally, we want to replace the proportionality symbol with an equality symbol. Let $k$ be a positive constant. Since the car's displacement *increases* with time, our derivative should be *positive*. Therefore, we can rewrite our proportionality statement as

$$
\frac{\text{d}D}{\text{d}t}=kt.
$$

q-79945.knowledge_point: Finding a Series Solution to a Second-Order Initial Value Problem About a Non-Zero Point
q-79945.problem:
Use the Taylor series method to find a series solution about $x=\pi $, in ascending powers of $(x-\pi )$ up to and including the term in $(x-\pi )^{3},$  of the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}={y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x,\,y(\pi )=1,\,{y}^{′}(\pi )=-1.
$$
q-79945.worked_solution:
We wish to express $y(x)$ as a Taylor series about $x=\pi $:

$$
y(x)=y(\pi )+(x-\pi ){y}^{′}(\pi )+\frac{(x-\pi )^{2}}{2!}{y}^{″}(\pi )+\frac{(x-\pi )^{3}}{3!}{y}^{(3)}(\pi )+⋯
$$

We're given $y(\pi )$ and ${y}^{′}(\pi ),$ so we need to calculate ${y}^{″}(\pi )$ and ${y}^{(3)}(\pi ).$

We substitute $y(\pi )=1$ into the given equation to find ${y}^{″}(\pi ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{″}(\pi ) & ={y}^{2}(\pi )\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi ) \\  & ={1}^{2}\cdot (0) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, to find an expression for ${y}^{(3)}(x),$ we differentiate both sides on the given equation with respect to $x:$ 

$$
{y}^{(3)}(x)=2y{y}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{y}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

We can now find  ${y}^{(3)}(\pi )$ by substituting in the known values:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{(3)}(\pi ) & =2y(\pi ){y}^{′}(\pi )\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )+{y}^{2}(\pi )\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi ) \\  & =2(1)(-1)(0)+(1)^{2}(-1) \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we  substitute  the obtained values in  the Taylor series:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =y(\pi )+(x-\pi ){y}^{′}(\pi )+\frac{(x-\pi )^{2}}{2!}{y}^{″}(\pi )+\frac{(x-\pi )^{3}}{3!}{y}^{(3)}(\pi )+⋯ \\  & =1+(x-\pi )\cdot (-1)+\frac{(x-\pi )^{2}}{2}\cdot (0)+\frac{(x-\pi )^{3}}{6}\cdot (-1)+… \\  & =1-(x-\pi )-\frac{1}{6}(x-\pi )^{3}+⋯\end{aligned}
$$

q-97990.knowledge_point: Finding the Principal Axes of a Quadratic Plane Curve Given the Corresponding Eigenvalues
q-97990.problem: Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]$ and the quadratic curve ${x}^{T}\,Ax=7.$ Given that $A$ has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,$ find the principal axes of the curve.
q-97990.worked_solution:
Notice that $A$ is symmetric. 
The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=7
$$

are the vectors that give an orthonormal eigenvector basis for $A.$ Let's now find these eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-3)I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]+3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-3)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$
